subtitle: Fix four small mistakes that attackers love: redirects, secret checks, logs and SQL.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 15. By the end you should be able to tell the story of each of the four attacks and name the one-line fix for each.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
A backend is open to the whole internet, so some requests come from **attackers**. Most attacks use small, ordinary mistakes, not clever magic.

Think of the locks on a house: none is complicated, but every door needs one. The rule behind all four: **never trust what comes in from outside**.
slides.notes: Same as data cleaning: a value a user typed is data to check, never an instruction to follow. Each of your four functions is one lock.

slides.title: New words

terms.meaning: A response that says "go to this other address instead".
Where to send the user after login: `/login?next=/tasks/`.
The website part of an address, like `backendlab.test`.
A long secret password that a program sends to prove who it is.
Anything that identifies a real person, like an email.
SQL with a `%s` placeholder; the value is passed **separately**.

slides.notes: A relative path like /dashboard/ has no host, so it always stays on your site. SQL is the language databases understand.

slides.title: Attack 1: the open redirect
slides.text: An attacker emails Ada a link: `backendlab.test/login?next=https://backendlab-login.evil.example`. It starts with your real site, so she logs in. Your site then sends her to the attacker's copy, which asks for her password again.
bullets: The link looked safe because it started with your address
**Fix:** only redirect to your own site; anything else goes to `/`
Your function: `safe_next_url(url, allowed_hosts)`
slides.notes: Phishers love these. The victim did everything right: she checked the link started with the real site.

slides.title: Attack 2: the timing attack
slides.text: A guard checks a password one letter at a time and says "wrong!" at the first mismatch. A wrong first letter gets a quick answer; a right one, a slightly slower one. By timing answers, an attacker guesses the secret **one letter at a time**.
bullets: Python's `==` on strings can behave like that guard
**Fix:** `hmac.compare_digest` always takes the same time
Your function: `api_key_matches(provided, expected)`
slides.notes: The differences are tiny, but attackers can send millions of requests and average the timings.

slides.title: Attack 3: personal data in logs
slides.text: Your app logs "Password reset for ada.lovelace@example.com". Logs get copied into tools, emailed around and kept for months. One day a log file leaks, and thousands of emails are public.
bullets: In many countries that is also against the law
**Fix:** mask it first: `a***@example.com` is still useful for debugging
Your function: `mask_email(email)`

slides.title: Attack 4: SQL injection
slides.text: A search box glues the typed title into SQL. Someone types `x' OR '1'='1`. The quote ends the title early, and the rest becomes **part of the command**: "title is x, OR 1 equals 1". Every task of every user comes back.
bullets: With other text, an attacker could even delete tables
**Fix:** pass the value separately, so it's treated as plain data
Your function: `find_tasks_by_title(title)`
slides.notes: Even without an attacker, gluing breaks: a title like Ada's task contains a quote and crashes the query. That's test 10.

slides.title: What your code receives and returns
slides.caption: The tests call your four functions with these values. `HOSTS` is `["backendlab.test"]`.
slides.code:
safe_next_url("/dashboard/", HOSTS)                  # "/dashboard/"
safe_next_url("https://evil.example/login", HOSTS)   # "/"
safe_next_url("//evil.example", HOSTS)               # "/"

api_key_matches("sk_live_abc123", "sk_live_abc123")  # True
api_key_matches("", "")                              # False: empty never matches

mask_email("ada.lovelace@example.com")               # "a***@example.com"
mask_email("not-an-email")                           # "***"

find_tasks_by_title("Deploy")                        # [1], the Deploy task's id
find_tasks_by_title("x' OR '1'='1")                  # [] (nothing has that title)
slides.notes: Also blocked: javascript:alert(1), empty and None addresses, and backendlab.test.evil.example, which only starts like ours. Test 5 checks that you really call hmac.compare_digest.

slides.title: Tool: url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme
slides.caption: Django's own "safe to redirect to?" **function**: address first, then the allowed hosts.
slides.code:
from django.utils.http import url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme
urls = ["/cart/", "https://shop.test/cart/",
        "https://evil.example/", "//evil.example"]
for url in urls:
    print(url, url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(url, allowed_hosts=["shop.test"]))
slides.output:
/cart/ True
https://shop.test/cart/ True
https://evil.example/ False
//evil.example False
slides.notes: It gives True or False, not an address. Your function must return url or "/". Don't write your own check: url.startswith("/") lets //evil.example through.

slides.title: Tools: not value and hmac.compare_digest
slides.caption: `not` catches empty and `None` at once; `compare_digest` compares **bytes** in constant time.
slides.code:
import hmac

print(not "", not None, not "abc")
print(hmac.compare_digest("tea".encode(), "tea".encode()))
print(hmac.compare_digest("tea".encode(), "tee".encode()))
slides.notes: Check for empty or None first: None.encode() crashes. .encode() turns text into bytes, which also handles accented letters.

slides.title: Tools: partition("@") and text[0]
slides.caption: `partition` always gives 3 pieces; a missing `@` leaves the last two empty.
slides.code:
print("tea@shop.test".partition("@"))
print("no-at-sign".partition("@"))
print("@shop.test".partition("@"))
print("tea"[0], repr(None or ""))    # handy trick: None or "" gives ""
slides.notes: You met partition in exercise 1. It crashes on None, which is why (value or "") is useful. text[0] is the first character.

slides.title: Gluing SQL vs a parameterised query

left.heading: f"... title = '{title}'"
bullets: The value is glued **into the SQL text**
A quote in it ends the string early
`x' OR '1'='1` becomes part of the command
`Ada's task` crashes the query

right.heading: cursor.execute(sql, [values])
bullets: Write a bare `%s` in the SQL, **no quotes**
Pass the values in a **separate list**
`"... WHERE id = %s", [pen.id]`
Quotes in the value are just letters

slides.notes: '%s' with quotes, or "..." % title, both glue the value in again. The ORM (Task.objects.filter(title=...)) always does it the safe way.

steps.text: `safe_next_url`: not empty and safe? Return `url`; otherwise `"/"`
`api_key_matches`: `if not provided or not expected:` return `False`
Otherwise first letter of `local` + `***@` + domain, with an f-string

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: `url.startswith("/")` as the check: `//evil.example` sneaks through
Returning `True`/`False` from `safe_next_url`: it must return an **address**
`provided == expected`: not constant time, and `"" == ""` is `True`
`email.split("@")` crashes on `None`; `partition` always gives 3 pieces
`'%s'` with quotes, or an f-string: the value must go in `[title]`

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: Django already protects you in many places: its login view checks `?next=` with the same function you used, and the ORM always uses parameterised queries. The danger is where you step **outside** that protection.
bullets: Raw SQL for a report: always pass values in the list
Checking a webhook's or partner's API key: `compare_digest`
Writing log lines about users: mask emails, never log passwords

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: Why is a link that starts with your real site still dangerous?
What does `==` leak about a secret that `compare_digest` doesn't?
In `x' OR '1'='1`, which character lets the text escape into the SQL?
